title: The Ruler Detector

scenario.situation: A skin-lesion classifier achieves 94% AUC on the held-out test set but malignant-detection accuracy drops sharply when deployed to partner clinics.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The team believes the model learned genuine pathological features — asymmetry, irregular borders, color variation — and that the clinic drop is due to lower image quality or different patient demographics.
scenario.question: Why does a high-AUC model fail in deployment, and what did it actually learn?

decisions.prompt: The team wants to close the gap between lab and clinic. How do you frame the investigation?

options.label: Audit clinic image quality
options.detail: Compare resolution, lighting, and camera specs between training images and clinic images.
options.consequence: You find minor resolution differences, but equalizing them doesn't recover performance. Image quality wasn't the gap — you've spent time on a distraction and still have no explanation.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the team's demographic/quality hypothesis and missed the actual signal in the training data.

options.label: Diagnostic slice analysis — split performance by image metadata
options.detail: Segment model performance by image-level metadata attributes (presence of artifacts, imaging context, collection site) to see where accuracy concentrates or collapses.
options.consequence: Slicing by metadata immediately surfaces a striking pattern: performance diverges sharply along an attribute that has nothing to do with lesion pathology. A real investigative thread opens that the quality hypothesis never would have found.

options.label: Collect more clinic data and retrain
options.detail: Gather a larger sample from clinic deployments and fine-tune the model on it.
options.consequence: Performance recovers slightly on the new clinic set, but you've patched a symptom without diagnosing the cause. The shortcut may persist, and the next deployment site could fail again.
options.divergenceCost: Treated the symptom instead of diagnosing the root cause — the model's learned representation is still unknown.

options.label: Run a benchmark against published dermatology models
options.detail: Compare DermaScan's model AUC to state-of-the-art models on a public dataset.
options.consequence: DermaScan's model competes well on the public benchmark — which shares the same data distribution problems. The comparison is flattering but tells you nothing about why it fails in clinics.
options.divergenceCost: Benchmarked on data with the same bias, confirming nothing meaningful about generalization.

decisions.prompt: Your metadata slice reveals that ruler presence varies systematically across classes. Which metric do you use to confirm it's driving predictions?

artifact.title: Malignant predictions by image attribute — raw counts
artifact.caption: Raw counts of malignant predictions per attribute group. Ruler images produce the most predictions — but ruler images are also far more common in the malignant training class. Is this risk or just volume?

options.label: Raw malignant-prediction counts by artifact group
options.detail: Count how many malignant predictions fall in each artifact category.
options.consequence: Ruler images produce the most malignant predictions — but ruler images are disproportionately represented in the malignant class to begin with. You're reading class imbalance, not model behavior.
options.divergenceCost: Compared raw prediction counts across unequal base rates — mistook class frequency for model bias.

options.label: Malignant prediction rate within each artifact group (normalized)
options.detail: Compute the fraction of images predicted malignant within each artifact group, controlling for true-label distribution.
options.consequence: Normalized, the signal is unmistakable: benign lesions photographed with a ruler are classified malignant at nearly the same rate as truly malignant lesions — while benign images without a ruler are classified correctly. The model is keying on the ruler, not the lesion.

artifact.title: Malignant prediction RATE by artifact group — benign images only (%)
artifact.caption: Among ground-truth benign images, ruler presence drives a 64% malignant prediction rate — nearly matching the true malignant base rate. The model learned ruler = malignant.

decisions.prompt: Ruler presence in benign images drives false-positive malignant predictions at 64%. What do you tell the team?

options.label: "The model learned rulers, not lesions — retrain without ruler images."
options.detail: Make the causal call and prescribe the fix.
options.consequence: Removing ruler images may reduce this specific shortcut, but you've prescribed a fix based on one identified artifact without checking whether other spurious correlates exist. The model could still be exploiting unreported shortcuts in the cleaned data.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed a complete causal explanation and prescribed a fix without ruling out other shortcuts.

options.label: "Ruler presence is the strongest spurious correlate we've found — this is consistent with shortcut learning, not pathology. Before retraining, we should apply attribution methods to verify what the model attends to, and test on a ruler-free holdout to confirm the shortcut is the dominant failure mode."
options.detail: Report the finding, name the mechanism, and recommend a causal confirmation step before acting.
options.consequence: The team now understands the mechanism, not just the symptom. Gradient attribution maps confirm the model highlights ruler pixels, not lesion regions. The ruler-free holdout collapses AUC from 0.94 to 0.61, cementing the diagnosis. Retraining is now targeted and justified.

insight: The classifier never learned dermatology — it learned that rulers appear in clinical photos taken of suspicious lesions, and exploited that artifact as a near-perfect proxy for malignancy. The lab test set had the same bias, so AUC looked excellent right up until deployment in ruler-free clinics. The lesson is that high held-out accuracy guarantees nothing about what a model actually learned; segmenting performance by image metadata and normalizing for base rates is what surfaces spurious shortcuts, and attribution methods plus distribution-shifted holdouts are the only way to confirm the fix.
